items.prompt: How does this unit define "appreciation", as distinct from a purchase decision?
choices: Recognizing something is well-built or impressive, without it being tied to a cost the buyer is already trying to reduce
The moment a buyer signs a contract
A discount offered to close a deal faster
The total number of features a product has
items.reference:
😮 Appreciation — 'that's impressive', no cost attached
💵 Conviction — a number, against a budget, worth acting on now

Why: a demo can produce admiration all day and never produce a sale, because admiration isn't a budget decision.
items.explanation: Appreciation is recognizing that something is clever or well-built without connecting it to a personal or organizational cost the buyer is already trying to reduce — a demo can produce appreciation without ever producing a sale.

items.prompt: In the invoice-reconciliation scenario, the finance director said 'that's genuinely impressive' after the first demo, then never followed up. What state had she reached?
choices: Conviction
Appreciation
A signed purchase order
Comprehension of a specific dollar figure
items.reference:
😮 Appreciation — 'that's impressive', no cost attached
💵 Conviction — a number, against a budget, worth acting on now

Why: a demo can produce admiration all day and never produce a sale, because admiration isn't a budget decision.
items.explanation: "That's genuinely impressive" with no follow-up is the textbook signature of appreciation — the director admired the capability but never connected it to a cost she was already trying to reduce, so nothing compelled her to act.

items.prompt: Why can a demo produce appreciation without ever leading to a sale?
choices: Because appreciation is a rare reaction most buyers never reach
Because admiring a product is a judgment about the product, not a budget decision about spending money on it
Because demos are always technically flawed
Because appreciation only happens when the price is too high
items.reference:
😮 Appreciation — 'that's impressive', no cost attached
💵 Conviction — a number, against a budget, worth acting on now

Why: a demo can produce admiration all day and never produce a sale, because admiration isn't a budget decision.
items.explanation: Admiring a product is a judgment that the product is good; a purchase requires a separate judgment that a specific cost is worth a specific outcome right now — appreciation alone never forces that second judgment to happen.

items.prompt: A prospect says 'I understand this could help our team.' Has this buyer reached conviction?
choices: Yes — understanding a benefit is the same as being ready to buy
No — this is comprehension, a general connection to a problem, not a specific number weighed against a budget
Yes, because they used the word 'help'
No, because they haven't seen a demo yet
items.reference:
🧠 Comprehension — 'I see the problem this solves', still general
💵 Conviction — a specific number against a specific budget

Why: understanding a benefit and being ready to commit budget to it are separate states.
items.explanation: "This could help our team" is comprehension — a general connection between the capability and a real problem — but it lacks the specific number weighed against a specific budget that conviction, and a purchase decision, actually requires.

items.prompt: What does "conviction" require that comprehension alone does not?
choices: A longer demo
A specific number, weighed against something the buyer already tracks, that clears a threshold worth acting on now
A lower price than any competitor
A signed reference from another customer
items.reference:
🧠 Comprehension — 'I see the problem this solves', still general
💵 Conviction — a specific number against a specific budget

Why: understanding a benefit and being ready to commit budget to it are separate states.
items.explanation: Conviction requires a number specific enough that the buyer can weigh it directly against their own budget or losses — comprehension only requires recognizing that the capability relates to a real problem, which is a much lower bar.

items.prompt: Why do most pitches stop at appreciation or comprehension instead of reaching conviction?
choices: Because most products aren't actually good enough to justify a purchase
Because they're built to impress or to explain, and treat conviction as if it follows automatically without a specific number
Because buyers are naturally reluctant to spend money on anything
Because conviction requires a live product demo, which most pitches skip
items.reference:
🧠 Comprehension — 'I see the problem this solves', still general
💵 Conviction — a specific number against a specific budget

Why: understanding a benefit and being ready to commit budget to it are separate states.
items.explanation: Most pitches are built to produce a good demo or a clear explanation, and treat comprehension and conviction as if they follow automatically from appreciation — they don't, because conviction specifically requires a number the buyer can weigh against their own budget.

items.prompt: How does this unit define "value-based selling"?
choices: Pricing and pitching a product based on the outcome it delivers, rather than what it contains or costs to build
Always selling at the lowest possible price to win the deal
Only pitching to buyers who already understand the product's technology
Bundling as many features as possible into one pitch
items.reference:
🎯 Value-based selling — anchor pitch and price to outcome delivered
🚫 Not what it contains, not what it cost to build

Why: the outcome case is what turns 'this will help' into a number the buyer can check against their own budget.
items.explanation: Value-based selling anchors the pitch and the price to the concrete outcome delivered — money saved, time recovered, risk avoided — rather than to the product's contents or build cost.

items.prompt: What is the actual mechanical skill this unit builds, on top of already knowing to lead with value instead of features?
choices: Writing better product documentation
Building a specific, defensible number the buyer can check against their own budget
Memorizing every competitor's pricing
Learning to speak faster during a pitch
items.reference:
🎯 Value-based selling — anchor pitch and price to outcome delivered
🚫 Not what it contains, not what it cost to build

Why: the outcome case is what turns 'this will help' into a number the buyer can check against their own budget.
items.explanation: This unit's specific territory is turning a value claim into a defensible number — the mechanics of quantification, not the general principle of leading with value, which a related unit already covers.

items.prompt: In L1's scenario, the two pitches described the exact same capability. What did the second pitch add that the first one didn't?
choices: A lower price
A number tied to something the buyer already measures, plus a timeframe
A longer, more detailed product demo
A discount for signing quickly
items.reference:
😮 Pitch 1: 'auto-reconciles invoices' → no sale
💰 Pitch 2: 'saves $48k/year, pays back in 7 weeks' → signed

Why: same feature, but only the second pitch gave the buyer a number to weigh against her own budget.
items.explanation: The second pitch added a number tied to something the director already tracks (labor cost) and a specific timeframe (seven weeks to break even) — the capability itself never changed.

items.prompt: Why did the same feature produce no sale in one pitch and a signed deal within the week in another?
choices: The second pitch used more technical jargon to sound credible
The framing changed from describing the capability to quantifying its effect on a number the buyer already owns
The second buyer had a bigger budget than the first
The second pitch happened in person instead of over video
items.reference:
😮 Pitch 1: 'auto-reconciles invoices' → no sale
💰 Pitch 2: 'saves $48k/year, pays back in 7 weeks' → signed

Why: same feature, but only the second pitch gave the buyer a number to weigh against her own budget.
items.explanation: It was the same director and the same feature — what changed was quantification: the second pitch converted a capability into its effect on a number the director already owns and is accountable for, which is what value-based selling means in practice.

items.prompt: According to this unit, what is a purchase decision actually a judgment about?
choices: Whether the product is technically well-built
Whether this specific cost, right now, is worth this specific outcome
Whether the sales rep is trustworthy
Whether the product has more features than competitors
items.reference:
❓ Not: 'is this a good product?'
✅ Actually: 'is this cost, now, worth this outcome?'

Why: a buyer can admire a product and never be asked this second, separate question.
items.explanation: A purchase decision is a judgment about whether a specific cost, right now, is worth a specific outcome — not a judgment about whether the product itself is good, which is a separate and easier bar to clear.

items.prompt: Why can a buyer complete the judgment 'this product is good' without ever completing the judgment 'this is worth paying for'?
choices: Because the two judgments require different information — one about the product, the other about a specific cost versus a specific outcome
Because buyers are always dishonest about their intentions
Because good products are never worth their price
Because the two judgments are actually the same thing
items.reference:
❓ Not: 'is this a good product?'
✅ Actually: 'is this cost, now, worth this outcome?'

Why: a buyer can admire a product and never be asked this second, separate question.
items.explanation: The two judgments draw on different information: whether a product is good is a judgment about the product itself, while whether it's worth paying for requires weighing a specific cost against a specific outcome — a pitch that only proves the first never forces the second.

items.prompt: What is the practical implication for a pitch, given that a purchase decision is a judgment about cost versus outcome, not just product quality?
choices: The pitch should spend more time proving the product works well
The pitch has to explicitly supply the cost-versus-outcome comparison — the buyer usually won't construct it unprompted
The pitch should avoid mentioning price at all
The pitch should focus entirely on the buyer's competitors
items.reference:
❓ Not: 'is this a good product?'
✅ Actually: 'is this cost, now, worth this outcome?'

Why: a buyer can admire a product and never be asked this second, separate question.
items.explanation: Since the two judgments are separate, a pitch that only demonstrates product quality never forces the cost-versus-outcome comparison a purchase actually requires — the pitch has to supply that comparison directly, because most buyers won't construct it on their own.

items.prompt: Put appreciation, comprehension, and conviction in the order this unit builds them, from weakest to strongest signal toward a purchase.
choices: Conviction, comprehension, appreciation
Appreciation, comprehension, conviction
Comprehension, appreciation, conviction
They have no meaningful order — all three are equivalent
items.reference:
1️⃣ Appreciation — 'that's clever'
2️⃣ Comprehension — 'I see the problem this solves'
3️⃣ Conviction — a number against a budget

Why: most pitches stall at stage 1 or 2 and never supply what stage 3 requires.
items.explanation: The order is appreciation (admiring the product) → comprehension (connecting it to a real, recognized problem) → conviction (a specific number against a specific budget) — most pitches are built to reach the first two and stall there.

items.prompt: Most pitches are built to produce which of the three states, according to this unit, while treating the others as automatic?
choices: Conviction
Appreciation
None of the three — most pitches aren't built to produce any of them
Comprehension only, never appreciation
items.reference:
1️⃣ Appreciation — 'that's clever'
2️⃣ Comprehension — 'I see the problem this solves'
3️⃣ Conviction — a number against a budget

Why: most pitches stall at stage 1 or 2 and never supply what stage 3 requires.
items.explanation: Most pitches are built around a good demo, which produces appreciation — a well-built, clever impression — and then treat comprehension and conviction as if they follow automatically, when each stage actually requires something the previous one doesn't supply.

items.prompt: What does comprehension require that appreciation alone does not?
choices: A lower price
Connecting the capability to a problem the buyer recognizes as genuinely their own
A written contract
A reference customer
items.reference:
1️⃣ Appreciation — 'that's clever'
2️⃣ Comprehension — 'I see the problem this solves'
3️⃣ Conviction — a number against a budget

Why: most pitches stall at stage 1 or 2 and never supply what stage 3 requires.
items.explanation: Comprehension requires connecting the capability to a problem the buyer recognizes as their own — appreciation only requires recognizing the product is well-built, with no requirement that the buyer see it as solving anything specific to them.

items.prompt: How does this unit define "cost of inaction"?
choices: The price of the product being sold
What the current, unsolved state of the problem is already costing the buyer, in their own units
The cost of onboarding a new tool
The cost of cancelling a contract early
items.reference:
🩸 Cost of inaction — what the status quo is already costing, right now
👀 Often invisible — the buyer is absorbing it as 'just how things are'

Why: naming this cost out loud is persuasive before the product is even mentioned.
items.explanation: Cost of inaction is what the current, unsolved state of the problem is already costing the buyer, expressed in units they already track — hours of labor, dollars lost to errors, revenue at risk.

items.prompt: Why is naming the cost of inaction out loud often persuasive on its own, before any product is even mentioned?
choices: Because it usually surprises the buyer with a lower number than they expected
Because the buyer is often absorbing that cost as 'just how things are' and has never seen it written down as a number
Because it makes the buyer feel guilty about wasting money
Because it's always a bigger number than the product's price
items.reference:
🩸 Cost of inaction — what the status quo is already costing, right now
👀 Often invisible — the buyer is absorbing it as 'just how things are'

Why: naming this cost out loud is persuasive before the product is even mentioned.
items.explanation: The cost of inaction often doesn't exist anywhere written down — the buyer has been absorbing it as normal, unavoidable overhead, so simply naming it as a real, countable cost is persuasive by itself, independent of whatever product is later proposed to fix it.

items.prompt: A finance director mentions, almost as an aside, that mismatched invoices occasionally get paid incorrectly and take half a day each to fix. Should this be included in the cost-of-inaction ledger?
choices: No — only the problem the buyer names first or most emphatically counts
Yes — cost of inaction is often hiding in exactly this kind of aside, not only in the headline complaint
No — rework costs are always cost of adoption, not cost of inaction
Yes, but only if the buyer explicitly labels it a 'cost'
items.reference:
🩸 Cost of inaction — what the status quo is already costing, right now
👀 Often invisible — the buyer is absorbing it as 'just how things are'

Why: naming this cost out loud is persuasive before the product is even mentioned.
items.explanation: Yes — cost of inaction is frequently found in an offhand mention rather than the buyer's headline complaint, which is exactly why a rep has to listen for it rather than only recording what the buyer explicitly frames as a problem.

items.prompt: What does an honest "cost of adoption" figure include, beyond the product's price?
choices: Nothing — the subscription price alone is the full cost of adoption
The real effort of onboarding, training, and any temporary disruption while the new approach beds in
Only the cost of cancelling if the buyer changes their mind later
The buyer's total annual revenue
items.reference:
💳 Price
🧑‍🏫 + Onboarding / training effort
📉 + Ramp-up dip while the team learns it

Why: leaving out the effort side makes a case look better than it will actually feel to live through.
items.explanation: Cost of adoption includes the product's price plus the real cost of onboarding, training, and any temporary productivity dip while the team learns the new approach — quoting only the sticker price understates it.

items.prompt: Why is leaving out onboarding and ramp-up effort from the cost-of-adoption figure a common way an ROI case looks better than reality?
choices: Because onboarding effort is usually negligible and doesn't matter
Because it hides real costs the buyer will still experience, making the payback period look shorter than it will actually feel
Because buyers never notice onboarding time
Because onboarding costs are always paid by the vendor, not the buyer
items.reference:
💳 Price
🧑‍🏫 + Onboarding / training effort
📉 + Ramp-up dip while the team learns it

Why: leaving out the effort side makes a case look better than it will actually feel to live through.
items.explanation: Onboarding and ramp-up effort are real costs the buyer will still experience regardless of whether the pitch mentions them — leaving them out of the ledger makes the payback period look shorter on paper than it will actually feel once the buyer lives through the switch.

items.prompt: How is "payback period" defined in this unit?
choices: The length of the sales contract
How long it takes for the savings from closing the cost-of-inaction gap to exceed the cost of adoption
The time between the first demo and the signed contract
The refund window if the buyer is unsatisfied
items.reference:
🩸 Cost of inaction
💳 Cost of adoption
⏱️ → Payback period

Why: this is usually the one number a buyer remembers from the whole pitch.
items.explanation: Payback period is how long it takes for the savings from closing the cost-of-inaction gap to exceed the cost of adoption — the point at which the switch has fully paid for itself.

items.prompt: Why is the payback period often the single number a buyer remembers from an entire pitch?
choices: Because it's always the largest number mentioned
Because it's concrete and time-bound in a way vaguer claims like 'significant savings' never are
Because it's the only number that's legally required to be disclosed
Because buyers are trained specifically to remember payback periods
items.reference:
🩸 Cost of inaction
💳 Cost of adoption
⏱️ → Payback period

Why: this is usually the one number a buyer remembers from the whole pitch.
items.explanation: "Seven weeks" is concrete and time-bound in a way "significant savings" never is — it gives the buyer a specific, checkable claim rather than a vague impression, which is why it tends to be the one figure that sticks.

items.prompt: Why does 'this saves your team a lot of time' tend to stall a conversation where 'this saves 14 hours a week, about $46,000 a year' doesn't?
choices: Because 'a lot' is technically inaccurate
Because the vague version gives the buyer nothing concrete to compare against their own budget, so there's nothing to act on
Because buyers dislike hearing the word 'a lot'
Because vague claims are always false
items.reference:
🌫️ Vague: 'saves a lot of time' → nothing to compare
🔢 Quantified: '14 hrs/wk, $46k/yr' → compares directly to buyer's own budget

Why: a specific number invites a specific, answerable objection — which is progress, not a setback.
items.explanation: A vague claim gives the buyer nothing precise enough to weigh against their own numbers, so the conversation has nowhere concrete to go — a quantified claim competes directly with the buyer's own budget and other spending priorities.

items.prompt: A quantified ROI claim often invites a specific objection, like 'where does 14 hours come from?' Is that objection a setback?
choices: Yes — any pushback means the pitch has failed
No — it's progress, because a specific number gives the buyer something real to test, and testing is how a number earns trust
Yes, because it means the number was wrong
No, but only because objections always end in a discount
items.reference:
🌫️ Vague: 'saves a lot of time' → nothing to compare
🔢 Quantified: '14 hrs/wk, $46k/yr' → compares directly to buyer's own budget

Why: a specific number invites a specific, answerable objection — which is progress, not a setback.
items.explanation: A specific objection is progress, not a setback — it means the buyer is actually evaluating the number rather than politely agreeing and moving on, and testing a number is exactly the process that leads to trusting it.

items.prompt: What does it mean that a claim never gets questioned by the buyer?
choices: It means the claim was perfectly convincing on its own merits
It may mean the claim was too vague or unimportant to be evaluated seriously in the first place
It always means the buyer is ready to sign
It means the rep undercharged for the product
items.reference:
🌫️ Vague: 'saves a lot of time' → nothing to compare
🔢 Quantified: '14 hrs/wk, $46k/yr' → compares directly to buyer's own budget

Why: a specific number invites a specific, answerable objection — which is progress, not a setback.
items.explanation: A claim too soft to disagree with is often a claim that was never precise enough to be taken seriously enough to evaluate — a claim that gets questioned is, paradoxically, more likely to have actually registered with the buyer.

items.prompt: In the worked cost-of-inaction ledger, the rep used the director's own stated hourly rate ($55/hr fully loaded) rather than a generic industry rate. Why does this matter?
choices: It doesn't matter — any reasonable rate produces the same result
It ties every line item back to a fact the buyer supplied herself, making the resulting number harder to dismiss as vendor-inflated
It matters only because it happened to produce a bigger number
It matters because industry rates are always illegal to quote
items.reference:
🧾 15 hrs/wk matching + rework → ≈$3,988/mo, buyer's own numbers

Why: a ledger built from the buyer's own facts is harder to dismiss than one built from vendor assumptions.
items.explanation: Building the ledger from the director's own stated rate and hours means every line traces back to a fact she supplied, not an assumption the rep imported — that's what makes the resulting total credible rather than easily dismissed as inflated.

items.prompt: What was the first question the rep asked the director, before quoting any figure, and why that question specifically?
choices: "Would this save you money?" — because it opens the conversation broadly
"How many people currently touch invoice matching, and roughly how much of their week does it take?" — because it asks for a fact she already has, not an estimate of a benefit she hasn't experienced
"What's your budget for this?" — because it qualifies the deal size immediately
"Have you seen our competitor's pricing?" — because it sets a comparison point
items.reference:
🧾 15 hrs/wk matching + rework → ≈$3,988/mo, buyer's own numbers

Why: a ledger built from the buyer's own facts is harder to dismiss than one built from vendor assumptions.
items.explanation: Asking how many people touch the process and roughly how much time it takes asks for a fact the director already has or can get quickly — a hypothetical question like "would this save you money" instead asks her to estimate a benefit she hasn't experienced yet, which she has no real basis to answer precisely.

items.prompt: Why did the honest cost-of-adoption figure include a 'ramp-up dip' for the first three weeks, even though it makes the case look slightly worse?
choices: Because vendors are legally required to disclose it
Because a buyer who lives through a rockier first month than promised stops trusting every other number in the pitch, even accurate ones
Because it has no real effect and was included only for appearances
Because it increases the price of the product
items.reference:
📉 Ramp-up: first 3 weeks at ~half eventual savings
⏱️ Real payback: ~7 weeks, not ~4.5 weeks

Why: a promise that doesn't match lived experience contaminates trust in every other number.
items.explanation: Including the ramp-up dip keeps the promise aligned with what the buyer will actually experience — if the pitch promised a shorter payback and reality took longer, that gap becomes evidence the rest of the numbers were optimistic too, damaging trust in the whole case, not just that one line.

items.prompt: Ignoring the ramp-up dip, the payback period was about four and a half weeks. Accounting for it honestly, it became just under seven weeks. Which number should the rep say out loud?
choices: About four and a half weeks — it's more impressive and closes deals faster
Just under seven weeks — it matches what the buyer will actually live through, keeping the case defensible after the sale
Neither — payback period should never be mentioned in a pitch
Whichever number the buyer's competitor was quoted
items.reference:
📉 Ramp-up: first 3 weeks at ~half eventual savings
⏱️ Real payback: ~7 weeks, not ~4.5 weeks

Why: a promise that doesn't match lived experience contaminates trust in every other number.
items.explanation: Just under seven weeks is the honest figure once the ramp-up dip is folded in — it's less dramatic, but it's what the buyer will actually experience, and a case that matches lived experience stays defensible after the sale instead of eroding trust the moment reality is checked.

items.prompt: The worked ledger has a cost of inaction of about $3,988/month and a subscription cost of $1,200/month. What does subtracting the second from the first represent?
choices: The total price of the product
The recurring monthly savings once the tool is fully adopted
The one-time onboarding cost
The buyer's total annual revenue
items.reference:
🩸 $3,988/mo cost of inaction
➖ $1,200/mo subscription
= $2,788/mo net recurring savings

Why: payback period is one-time adoption cost divided by this recurring savings figure.
items.explanation: Cost of inaction minus the recurring subscription cost gives the net monthly savings once the tool is running at full effect — here, roughly $2,788 a month — which is the figure the one-time adoption costs are measured against to derive the payback period.

items.prompt: In the worked example, why did the rep fold the ramp-up dip specifically into month one, rather than treating the payback calculation as a clean division of one-time cost by full monthly savings?
choices: To make the payback period look shorter
Because the ramp-up dip is real and happens during month one, so ignoring it would understate how long payback actually takes
Because month one is legally required to be treated differently
It made no actual difference to the final number
items.reference:
🩸 $3,988/mo cost of inaction
➖ $1,200/mo subscription
= $2,788/mo net recurring savings

Why: payback period is one-time adoption cost divided by this recurring savings figure.
items.explanation: The ramp-up dip is a real cost that happens during month one, not a hypothetical — folding it in there instead of assuming full savings from day one keeps the derived payback period (just under seven weeks) accurate to what the buyer will actually experience, rather than a cleaner but overly optimistic number.

items.prompt: What two figures does the payback period calculation ultimately compare?
choices: The product's price and the buyer's total revenue
The one-time cost of adoption and the net recurring monthly savings
The number of features and the number of competitors
The length of the sales cycle and the size of the deal
items.reference:
🩸 $3,988/mo cost of inaction
➖ $1,200/mo subscription
= $2,788/mo net recurring savings

Why: payback period is one-time adoption cost divided by this recurring savings figure.
items.explanation: Payback period compares the one-time cost of adoption (onboarding, ramp-up) against the net recurring monthly savings (cost of inaction minus subscription cost) — it's how long the recurring savings take to cover the one-time cost of switching.

items.prompt: A rep uses a generic industry benchmark to claim $92,000 in annual savings, nearly double the honest, buyer-specific figure of about $48,000. The director's team later confirms real savings closer to $30,000. What was the actual cost of the inflated claim?
choices: None — $30,000 in real savings is still a good outcome, so nothing was lost
Lost credibility on every future claim from that vendor, even accurate ones, not the loss of the deal itself
The vendor was legally required to issue a refund
The buyer immediately cancelled the contract
items.reference:
📈 Inflated: $92k promised (benchmark) → $30k real → trust broken
📊 Conservative: $48k promised (buyer's own numbers) → close to real → trust builds

Why: a defensible number the buyer can poke holes in and still find convincing beats an aggressive one.
items.explanation: The inflated claim's cost wasn't losing the deal — the buyer stayed a customer — it was that every future number from that vendor got discounted, and the director brought a colleague to sanity-check the next renewal and mentioned the gap unprompted to a peer, which taxes every future interaction.

items.prompt: Why does this unit argue that a conservative, defensible ROI number beats an aggressive one, even though the aggressive number is more impressive in the first meeting?
choices: Because conservative numbers are always more accurate by definition
Because the aggressive number wins the first meeting and loses every meeting after it, while the conservative number keeps paying off as it's checked
Because buyers always prefer round numbers
Because conservative numbers require less math to calculate
items.reference:
📈 Inflated: $92k promised (benchmark) → $30k real → trust broken
📊 Conservative: $48k promised (buyer's own numbers) → close to real → trust builds

Why: a defensible number the buyer can poke holes in and still find convincing beats an aggressive one.
items.explanation: The aggressive number does more work up front but breaks trust once checked against reality — the conservative number does slightly less work in the first meeting but holds up under scrutiny, which keeps paying off in every renewal, expansion, or reference conversation that follows.

items.prompt: The buyer stayed a customer even after discovering the real savings were $30,000, well under the promised $92,000. Was the inflated pitch still a mistake?
choices: No — since the buyer didn't leave, the pitch achieved its goal
Yes — the cost showed up as lost trust taxing every future interaction, not as a lost sale, and the padding was never needed to close a $30,000-worthy deal in the first place
No, because $92,000 was technically an achievable number under different conditions
Yes, but only because the vendor broke a legal disclosure requirement
items.reference:
📈 Inflated: $92k promised (benchmark) → $30k real → trust broken
📊 Conservative: $48k promised (buyer's own numbers) → close to real → trust builds

Why: a defensible number the buyer can poke holes in and still find convincing beats an aggressive one.
items.explanation: Yes — staying a customer isn't the same as the pitch working as intended. The real $30,000 result was sellable on its own; the extra padding never earned the deal, it only cost trust once checked, which is a real cost even though it didn't show up as a lost sale.

items.prompt: A buyer pushes back on a cost-of-inaction estimate: 'I don't think we're spending that much time on this.' What is the recommended response?
choices: Defend the original number more insistently until the buyer agrees
Make the number smaller and more verifiable — offer a source the buyer trusts more, or an explicitly conservative range that still clears the bar
Withdraw the pitch entirely and move on to a different prospect
Ignore the objection and continue with the rest of the pitch as planned
items.reference:
🤔 Buyer pushes back on a number
✅ Response: shrink it, verify it — don't defend it harder

Why: a number that survives being pressure-tested is trusted more than one that was never questioned.
items.explanation: The honest response is to make the number smaller and more verifiable rather than more insistent — offering a source the buyer trusts more, like their own time log, or a conservative range that still clears the bar, treats skepticism as a chance to demonstrate the number is real.

items.prompt: Why does a buyer who pressure-tests a number and watches it hold (or watches the rep willingly shrink it) end up trusting the final figure more than a buyer who never questioned it?
choices: Because questioning a number always makes it smaller
Because scrutiny that a number survives is direct evidence the number is real, which a number that was never checked hasn't earned
Because buyers who ask questions are easier to close overall
Because it means the rep is more experienced
items.reference:
🤔 Buyer pushes back on a number
✅ Response: shrink it, verify it — don't defend it harder

Why: a number that survives being pressure-tested is trusted more than one that was never questioned.
items.explanation: A number that's been pressure-tested and either held up or been honestly revised has earned trust through evidence — a number nobody questioned hasn't been through that process at all, so its credibility is untested, not necessarily higher.

items.prompt: The honest ledger comes out to a 14-month payback period instead of a dramatic one. What is the recommended move?
choices: Pad the cost-of-inaction figures until the payback period looks shorter and more urgent
State the real 14-month figure directly and, if genuine, pair it with a legitimate non-financial value such as reduced risk
Avoid quoting any payback period at all if it isn't impressive
Switch to pitching a completely different product
items.reference:
⏱️ Real payback: 14 months, not dramatic
🛡️ + honest secondary value (e.g. reduced compliance risk)

Why: padding a modest case is the same mistake as the industry-benchmark pitch, just smaller in scale.
items.explanation: The honest move is to state the real 14-month figure directly, and if there's a genuine secondary value (like reduced compliance risk), name it as exactly that — a legitimate secondary benefit alongside a modest financial case — rather than inflating the financial number to manufacture urgency.

items.prompt: Why is quietly inflating a genuine 14-month payback case into a fake seven-week one the same mistake as the industry-benchmark example, just smaller in scale?
choices: Because both involve a number disconnected from what the buyer's own situation actually supports, risking the same trust damage once checked
Because both are illegal under the same regulation
Because a 14-month payback is always a bad deal regardless of framing
Because both mistakes only affect the size of the commission, not the buyer

items.explanation: Both cases replace a number grounded in the buyer's actual situation with a more flattering one that isn't — the scale differs (a whole benchmark swap versus quietly reshaping one case) but the underlying failure, and the trust risk once the buyer checks it, is the same.
